prompt:
You maintain a running summary of a long engineering document that is being read part by part, so that a later reader can model the system in SysML v2 without seeing the earlier parts.
Update the summary with the new part. Keep, as compactly as possible: the full names of system elements, actors and items; every alias or call sign with the full name it stands for; which element produces, sends or receives which item; modes and normative requirements. At most 300 words.

Current summary:
Document: Management by Trajectory (MBT) Concept of Operations (ConOps), far-term ATM vision for the National Airspace System (NAS); interprets Trajectory Based Operations (TBO), consistent with ICAO TBO Concept. Far-term: NAS and most aircraft support Aeronautical Telecommunications Network-Baseline 2 (ATN-B2). Near-term constrained by NAS Enterprise Architecture (EA)/NextGen. Current NAS: automation predicts trajectories from flight plans; controllers issue open tactical clearances; Time Based Flow Management (TBFM). MBT: FAA and airspace users negotiate closed four-dimensional trajectories (4DTs) for all IFR aircraft; aircraft shall follow assigned 4DTs. NAS Constraint Service publishes constraints; traffic management automation translates TMIs into flight-specific constraints; aircraft send 4DT intent; conflicts resolved by modifying constraints. Data comm delivers 4DTs to Flight Management System (FMS); electronic flight bag (EFB). Negotiating controller coordinates with traffic management coordinators (TMCs). Near-term: controllers retain separation; one FMS Required Time of Arrival (RTA); CPDLC; SWIM; mixed equipage. Far-term: trajectories delivered digitally; voice for immediate action; TCAS/ACAS evolves from UAS detect-and-avoid, converging with Advanced Interval Management (A-IM); aircraft send planned avoidance maneuvers to ground automation. TBFM extends into en route; miles-in-trail (MIT) eliminated. Required Time Performance (RTP) complements Required Navigation Performance (RNP) for time-of-arrival control (TOAC); RTP-Y = 95% crossing-time error interval (s). All aircraft shall be certified to some RTP level. Flight operations centers, apps, private service providers; new users: on-demand, personal mobility, UAS, space launch/return, airships, rotorcraft. Scope: airborne only; surface MBT not pursued unless justified (compatible with closed surface TBO). Surface interface: ATM may plan pushback times from scheduled takeoff times and runway queue management; exchange takeoff/landing time predictions, runway assignments, departure/arrival transitions in assigned trajectory consistent with surface management plan. Traffic Flow Management (TFM) is separate: selects traffic management initiatives (TMIs) imposing trajectory constraints; MBT assigns TMI-compliant trajectories, modifies them as constraints change, ensures satisfaction; better predictability improves TMIs. Ground Delay Programs (GDPs)/Airspace Flow Programs (AFPs): near-term unchanged

New part:
U0101: The operator will have flexibility to determine when the aircraft takes off, depending on how fast or slow it wants to fly to conform with the CTA and how the takeoff time will affect other constraints.
U0102: Mile-in-trail and minute-in-trail (MINIT) restrictions will be reduced in the near term and eventually eliminated as unnecessary when flights are following 4DTs that include time-based constraints where necessary.
U0103: Increased use of self-separation techniques (e.g., A-IM) will allow efficient management of aircraft merging to a runway or other constrained airspace resource, without needing to repeatedly update time constraints in the assigned trajectories in response to residual uncertainty.
U0104: By keeping all flights on closed trajectories that are de-conflicted over at least the next 30 minutes, MBT may increase sector capacities.
U0105: Uncertainty, which MBT will reduce, hampers current TFM performance.
U0106: However, many TFM processes take advantage of the flexibility in current operations.
U0107: In any TBO environment, if aircraft are more predictable and are scheduled accordingly, the reduction in uncertainty may be accompanied by a reduction in flexibility.
U0108: However, some residual uncertainty will persist, creating the possibility that the TFM system might be more fragile to the remaining uncertainty.
U0109: One area in which research will be required to validate the MBT concept is how TFM must adjust to the tradeoff between uncertainty and flexibility to achieve the anticipated TFM benefits.
U0110: For example, if TFM continues to be conservative and initially absorb less delay than it expects will be required, to leave flexibility to fill an empty slot caused by another flight being late, then most flights will need their assigned trajectories to be updated, potentially multiple times, as the TFM system “releases” more and more of the expected necessary delay to the flights.

Return JSON {"summary": "..."}.
